definition: A step-by-step set of rules for solving a problem or completing a task.
exampleSentence: The app uses an algorithm to recommend new songs.
etymology: From the name of 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi, Latinized as 'Algoritmi'.

definition: A point where two systems meet and interact, especially between a user and a device.
exampleSentence: The new interface makes the software much easier to use.
etymology: Coined in the 1880s from 'inter-' (between) + 'face'.

definition: The process of converting information into a secret code to prevent unauthorized access.
exampleSentence: End-to-end encryption keeps your messages private.
etymology: From Greek 'kryptos' meaning hidden, via 'encrypt' plus '-ion'.

definition: The capacity of a network to transmit data, or one's capacity to handle tasks.
exampleSentence: Streaming video uses a lot of bandwidth.
etymology: Compound of 'band' (range of frequencies) + 'width', from early radio engineering.

definition: An organized collection of data stored for easy access and management.
exampleSentence: Customer records are kept in a secure database.
etymology: Compound of 'data' + 'base', first used in the 1960s computing era.

definition: A security system that monitors and controls network traffic.
exampleSentence: The company's firewall blocks suspicious connections.
etymology: Originally a physical wall to stop fire spreading; adopted by computing in the 1980s.

definition: A set of rules governing the exchange of data between devices.
exampleSentence: The internet relies on protocols like TCP/IP.
etymology: From Greek 'protokollon' meaning the first sheet glued to a manuscript.

definition: A temporary store of data that speeds up future requests.
exampleSentence: Clearing the cache often fixes loading problems.
etymology: From French 'cacher' meaning to hide.

definition: An error or flaw in a computer program.
exampleSentence: The update fixed a bug that crashed the app.
etymology: Popularized in 1947 when engineers found an actual moth jamming a relay in a computer.

definition: A computer that provides data or services to other computers on a network.
exampleSentence: The website went down when the server crashed.
etymology: From 'serve' + '-er' — a machine that 'serves' requests.

definition: To deliberately slow down a data connection or process.
exampleSentence: The provider throttles speeds after you use your monthly limit.
etymology: From Middle English 'throtelen' meaning to choke — applied to limiting flow.

definition: The delay before a transfer of data begins following an instruction.
exampleSentence: Low latency is crucial for online gaming.
etymology: From Latin 'latentia' meaning a lying hidden — from 'latere' (to lie hidden).

definition: The smallest unit of a digital image displayed on a screen.
exampleSentence: Zoom in far enough and you'll see individual pixels.
etymology: Blend of 'picture' (pix) + 'element' (el), coined in the 1960s.

definition: An early model of a product built to test a concept.
exampleSentence: They built a prototype before mass production.
etymology: From Greek 'prototypon' — 'proto' (first) + 'typos' (model).

definition: The use of machines or software to perform tasks with minimal human help.
exampleSentence: Automation has transformed modern factories.
etymology: From Greek 'automatos' meaning self-acting, via 'automatic' + '-ion'.

definition: The smallest unit of a chemical compound that retains its properties.
exampleSentence: A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
etymology: From Latin 'molecula', diminutive of 'moles' meaning mass.

definition: A proposed explanation made as a starting point for further investigation.
exampleSentence: The experiment was designed to test her hypothesis.
etymology: From Greek 'hypothesis' meaning a placing under — 'hypo' (under) + 'thesis' (placing).

definition: A community of living organisms interacting with their environment.
exampleSentence: Coral reefs form one of the richest ecosystems on Earth.
etymology: Coined in 1935 from 'eco-' (from Greek 'oikos', house) + 'system'.

definition: The quantity of motion of a moving body; figuratively, driving force.
exampleSentence: The campaign gained momentum after the debate.
etymology: From Latin 'momentum' meaning movement or moving power.

definition: The resistance one surface meets when moving over another; also conflict between people.
exampleSentence: Friction between the tires and road lets a car stop.
etymology: From Latin 'frictio' meaning a rubbing — from 'fricare' (to rub).

definition: An individual living thing, such as an animal, plant, or microbe.
exampleSentence: Even the simplest organism is astonishingly complex.
etymology: From Greek 'organon' meaning instrument or organ, via 'organize'.

definition: The gradual development of species over generations; any gradual change.
exampleSentence: Evolution explains the diversity of life on Earth.
etymology: From Latin 'evolutio' meaning an unrolling — of a scroll.

definition: The speed of something in a given direction.
exampleSentence: The rocket reached escape velocity in minutes.
etymology: From Latin 'velocitas' meaning swiftness — from 'velox' (swift).

definition: A substance that speeds up a reaction; figuratively, an agent of change.
exampleSentence: The discovery was a catalyst for an entire new field.
etymology: From Greek 'katalysis' meaning dissolution — 'kata' (down) + 'lysis' (loosening).

definition: A band of colors or a range of related qualities or ideas.
exampleSentence: Opinions covered the whole political spectrum.
etymology: From Latin 'spectrum' meaning an appearance or image — from 'specere' (to look).

definition: An individual example or sample used for study.
exampleSentence: The museum displays a rare specimen of the species.
etymology: From Latin 'specimen' meaning a mark or example — from 'specere' (to look).

definition: The combination of parts to form a connected whole.
exampleSentence: Her essay was a clever synthesis of several theories.
etymology: From Greek 'synthesis' — 'syn' (together) + 'thesis' (placing).

definition: Energy emitted as waves or particles.
exampleSentence: The sun gives off both light and harmful radiation.
etymology: From Latin 'radiatio' meaning a shining — from 'radius' (ray).

definition: A figure of speech describing one thing as if it were another.
exampleSentence: "Time is a thief" is a classic metaphor.
etymology: From Greek 'metaphora' meaning a transfer — 'meta' (across) + 'pherein' (to carry).

definition: A spoken or written account of connected events; a story.
exampleSentence: The film weaves three narratives into one.
etymology: From Latin 'narrativus' meaning telling a story — from 'narrare' (to recount).

definition: The leading character in a story.
exampleSentence: The protagonist must overcome her fear to save the town.
etymology: From Greek 'protagonistes' — 'protos' (first) + 'agonistes' (actor, combatant).

definition: Expression where the intended meaning is opposite to the literal words.
exampleSentence: It was a delicious irony that the fire station burned down.
etymology: From Greek 'eironeia' meaning feigned ignorance.

definition: A category of artistic work marked by a particular style or form.
exampleSentence: Science fiction is her favorite genre.
etymology: From French 'genre' meaning kind or sort — from Latin 'genus'.

definition: Ordinary written language without metrical structure, as opposed to poetry.
exampleSentence: Her prose is clear and elegant.
etymology: From Latin 'prosa (oratio)' meaning straightforward speech.

definition: Writing arranged with a metrical rhythm; poetry.
exampleSentence: He wrote the whole letter in verse.
etymology: From Latin 'versus' meaning a turning of the plow — and so a line of writing.

definition: A story whose characters and events symbolize a deeper meaning.
exampleSentence: The novel is an allegory of political corruption.
etymology: From Greek 'allegoria' meaning speaking otherwise — 'allos' (other) + 'agoreuein' (to speak).

definition: The most intense, decisive point of a story or event.
exampleSentence: The chase scene is the climax of the film.
etymology: From Greek 'klimax' meaning ladder or staircase.

definition: To hint at or warn of a future event in a story.
exampleSentence: The storm in chapter one foreshadows the tragedy to come.
etymology: Compound of 'fore-' (before) + 'shadow' — casting a shadow ahead.

definition: A grouped set of lines in a poem, like a paragraph.
exampleSentence: The poem's final stanza repeats the opening line.
etymology: From Italian 'stanza' meaning a stopping place or room.

definition: The use of humor or exaggeration to criticize people's faults.
exampleSentence: The show is a sharp satire of office life.
etymology: From Latin 'satira' meaning a medley or mixture.

definition: A short, often amusing true story about a real incident.
exampleSentence: She opened the speech with a charming anecdote.
etymology: From Greek 'anekdota' meaning things unpublished — 'an-' (not) + 'ekdotos' (given out).

definition: A system of government in which power rests with the people through voting.
exampleSentence: A free press is essential to any healthy democracy.
etymology: From Greek 'demokratia' — 'demos' (people) + 'kratos' (power).

definition: A system ranking people or things by status or authority.
exampleSentence: She quickly climbed the company hierarchy.
etymology: From Greek 'hierarkhia' — 'hieros' (sacred) + 'arkhein' (to rule).

definition: The health, happiness, and well-being of a person or group; government aid.
exampleSentence: The charity works for the welfare of refugees.
etymology: From Middle English 'wel faren' meaning to fare well.

definition: A social or religious custom forbidding a particular practice or topic.
exampleSentence: Discussing salaries is still a taboo in many offices.
etymology: From Tongan 'tabu' meaning forbidden — brought to English by Captain Cook in 1777.

definition: Movement of people or animals from one region to another.
exampleSentence: Mass migration reshaped the city's culture.
etymology: From Latin 'migratio' meaning a removal — from 'migrare' (to move).

definition: A decision reached by a jury or a judgment on a matter.
exampleSentence: The jury reached a unanimous verdict.
etymology: From Latin 'vere dictum' meaning truly said.

definition: A formal agreement between states or parties.
exampleSentence: The two nations signed a peace treaty.
etymology: From Old French 'traité', from Latin 'tractatus' meaning a handling or discussion.

definition: An official count of a population.
exampleSentence: The census is taken every ten years.
etymology: From Latin 'census', the registration of citizens in ancient Rome.

definition: A system of government or administration with many rules and officials.
exampleSentence: Getting the permit meant fighting endless bureaucracy.
etymology: From French 'bureau' (desk, office) + Greek 'kratos' (power) — rule by the desk.

definition: An official penalty, or conversely, official approval.
exampleSentence: Trade sanctions were imposed on the regime.
etymology: From Latin 'sanctio' meaning a binding law — from 'sancire' (to make sacred).

definition: Public support for a cause or policy.
exampleSentence: Her advocacy for clean water changed the town.
etymology: From Latin 'advocatus' meaning one called to aid — from 'advocare' (to summon).

definition: A particular section of a population grouped by shared traits.
exampleSentence: The product targets a young urban demographic.
etymology: From Greek 'demos' (people) + 'graphein' (to write).

definition: The basic physical systems of a society, such as roads and power.
exampleSentence: The country invested heavily in digital infrastructure.
etymology: From Latin 'infra' (below) + 'structure' — coined in early 20th-century French.
